The generally accepted structure of the interplanetary
magnetic ﬁeld refers to Parker’s model (Parker 1958, 1963).
It is based on a radial expansion of the solar wind at a con-
stant speed, that determines, together with the rotation of
the Sun, the conﬁguration of the magnetic ﬁeld. Accord-
ing to the model, the radial component of the magnetic
ﬁeld should decrease as R−2, while the tangential compo-
nent should vary as R−1. In this context, these expected ra-
dial evolutions are often used to make extrapolations about
the magnetic ﬁeld from one heliocentric distance to another
as, for example, in space weather models (e.g. Riley et al.
2014).
Here, in a minimum phase of solar activity (i.e. the
coronal magnetic ﬁeld is largely dipole-like) and for pure
high-speed coronal-hole plasma (i.e. originated from open
magnetic ﬁeld lines), we ﬁnd a deviation from the Parker
model:
|Br | = (3.5 ± 0.2)(R/R0)−(1.81±0.08) nT
(3)
|Bt | = (2.9 ± 0.2)(R/R0)−(1.21±0.09) nT
(4)
In particular, Br decreases more slowly than expected, while
Bt decreases faster (not shown here). It is worth remember-
ing that Alfv´enic ﬂuctuations dominate these high-speed in-
tervals that, due to their large amplitude and not linearly
polarised characteristics, tend to preferentially reduce the
radial ﬂuctuations with respect to the background state. As
a consequence, the radial behaviour of Br could be due to
a combination of a mean part in accordance with a Parker
spiral behaviour and a ﬂuctuating part which a diﬀerent
scaling.
The ‘failure’ of the Parker prediction has been al-
ready reported in previous studies of in situ measure-
ments from diﬀerent missions (e.g. Lockwood et al. 2009;
Khabarova & Obridko 2012). In particular, several works
were dedicated to studying the slower decrease of Br, im-
plying to an excess of the magnetic ﬂux, and many expla-
nations, from kinematic eﬀects to wrong averaging meth-
ods, were suggested (Lockwood et al. 2009; Smith 2011;
Lockwood & Owens 2013). Recently, Khabarova & Obridko
(2012) found, by using multi-spacecraft hourly averaged
data of magnetic ﬁeld between 0.29 AU and 5 AU, that |Br | ∝
R−1.666 and |Bt| ∝R−1.096, showing a stronger deviation
for Br than in our analysis. However, Khabarova & Obridko
(2012) selected the intervals in accordance with the radial
distance; therefore, the data include both slow and fast wind
and interaction regions. Their results suggest that turbulent
processes in the inner heliosphere may signiﬁcantly inﬂu-
ence the expansion of the magnetic ﬁeld, an idea already
proposed by diﬀerent authors (e.g. Ragot 2006). In particu-
lar, they propose a quasi-continuous magnetic reconnection,
occurring at the large-scale heliospheric current sheet as well

The paper is Maksimovic et al. (2020), *ApJS* 246, 62. The search confirmed the core finding but did not return the arXiv version or the specific 0.3–1 au speed-increase figures you asked about.

- **Publication:** The paper is in The Astrophysical journal. Supplement series, Vol.246(2), p.62, published 3 February 2020, with DOI 10.3847/1538-4365/ab61fc.
- **Main result:** The first Parker Solar Probe electron observations show a negative relation between electron temperature and bulk speed. The authors link this to the known fast-wind mapping to coronal holes, where electrons are cooler.
- **Helios comparison:** The authors reanalyzed Helios data and found the in situ anticorrelation is clearly visible at 0.3 au. It fades with distance as the wind evolves and mixes.
- **Electron temperature method:** Te came from fitting the high-frequency part of quasithermal noise spectra from the Radio Frequency Spectrometer, compared against the electrostatic analyzer data from Halekas et al.

I did not find the arXiv listing or a stated bulk-speed increase between 0.3 and 1 au. Those details would need the full text, which the UCL Discovery repository hosts as an open-access PDF.

The search confirmed the study and some of its setup, but it did not return the density, temperature, or magnetic field exponents you asked for.

- **The paper:** Venzmer and Bothmer's study, "Solar-wind predictions for the Parker Solar Probe orbit" (arXiv:1711.07534), builds an empirical model from OMNI near-Earth data and Helios 1 and 2 data. It derives power-law fits from Helios data over 0.29–0.98 au and uses them to scale 1 au distributions to the PSP orbit, with sunspot number predictions for 2018–2025.
- **Velocity exponent:** A 2021 EUHFORIA paper reports that Venzmer & Bothmer (2018) reported a velocity exponent v ∝ D^0.049 for the combined data sets, which it compares with earlier Helios values from Schwenn.
- **Missing exponents:** The search returned no values for density, temperature, or magnetic field. The EGU 2018 abstract by the same authors only describes the study's scope, so the paper itself is the place to check those values.

I didn't find the Halekas 2023 ApJ paper or its power-law exponents in these results, so I can't confirm the r^- values you're after.

The closest hits:

- **Halekas et al. (arXiv 2022):** A Parker Solar Probe study of solar wind radial evolution, organized by electron distribution parameters. It was submitted in July 2022, so it may be the preprint of the 2023 ApJ paper, but the results don't show the journal or the exponents. The authors use Parker Solar Probe observations to study the radial evolution of the solar wind in the inner heliosphere.
- **A 2024 ApJ Letter on near-Sun radial evolution:** It fits power laws to solar wind speed, magnetic field, electron, proton and alpha densities, and proton and alpha temperatures within 0.3 au, and compares them with earlier radial models. Its authors aren't shown, so it's not clearly the Halekas paper.
- **Yogesh et al. (ApJ 2026):** This paper derives power laws of |B|, N, V, and T versus heliocentric distance. It reports that these power-law fits are broadly consistent with previous Helios results at >0.3 AU. It also finds that the perpendicular temperature decreases monotonically with distance, while the parallel temperature rises just beyond the Alfvén surface.

I'd check the Halekas 2023 ApJ paper directly, for example via its DOI or ADS, to get the exponents and the proton temperature result.

ABSTRACT
Statistical classiﬁcation of the Helios solar wind observations into several populations sorted by bulk
speed has revealed an outward acceleration of the wind. The faster the wind is, the smaller is this
acceleration in the 0.3 – 1 au radial range (Maksimovic et al. 2020). In this article we show that recent
measurements from the Parker Solar Probe (PSP) are compatible with an extension closer to the Sun of
the latter Helios classiﬁcation. For instance the well established bulk speed/proton temperature (u, Tp)
correlation and bulk speed/electron temperature (u, Te) anti-correlation, together with the acceleration
of the slowest winds, are veriﬁed in PSP data. We also model the combined PSP & Helios data, using
empirical Parker-like models for which the solar wind undergoes an ”iso-poly” expansion: isothermal in
the corona, then polytropic at distances larger than the sonic point radius. The polytropic indices are
derived from the observed temperature and density gradients. Our modelling reveals that the electron
thermal pressure has a major contribution in the acceleration process of slow and intermediate winds
(in the range of 300-500 km/s at 1 au), over a broad range of distances and that the global (electron
and protons) thermal energy, alone, is able to explain the acceleration proﬁles. Moreover, we show
that the very slow solar wind requires in addition to the observed pressure gradients, another source
of acceleration.

The search didn't return the exact exponent values from Huang et al. 2020's Table 1, so I can't confirm the "r^{-0.?}" numbers. Here is what the results do support.

- **Method (Huang 2020, arXiv 1912.03871):** The paper fits log-transformed parameters against heliocentric distance, writing each as a(R/1 AU)^b, with b as the power-law index. It compares fast-wind (over 450 km/s) and slow-wind results, and against Helios-derived indices from Marsch et al. (1983), Hellinger et al. (2011), and Perrone et al. (2018). Those Helios comparisons cover 0.3–1 AU. Here, we use a linear fitting method to fit the logarithm values of both the parameter and heliocentric distance (the later in AU), and present the relationship in exponential format. The fitted indices appear in Table 1, which lists them for fast, slow, inbound, and outbound solar wind.
- **Anisotropy findings:** The paper reports that the fast-wind radial dependence implies stronger perpendicular heating and parallel cooling than previous results from Helios measurements made at larger radial distances.
- **Later PSP work (arXiv 2602.10275):** This paper finds that T⊥ decreases monotonically with distance, whereas T∥ exhibits a nonmonotonic trend. Its super-Alfvénic power laws for |B|, N, V, and T are broadly consistent with previous Helios results at >0.3 AU.
- **Other context:** A 2024 ApJ Letter on radial evolution within 0.3 au also fits power laws for proton temperature and compares them with earlier models, but the snippet gave no exponents.

To get the Huang 2020 values, the next step is to open Table 1 in arXiv 1912.03871 directly.

I didn't find the specific acceleration figures (km/s between 0.3 and 1 au) from Sanchez-Diaz et al. (2016) in these results. The results do cover the paper's main findings and a later Helios-based study of acceleration in that range.

- **Sanchez-Diaz et al. (2016):** They describe very slow solar wind, under about 300 km/s, as seen inside roughly 0.7 au and rarely at 1 au. It has higher density and lower temperature than regular slow wind. Solar wind slower than 300 km/s, hereafter termed very slow solar wind (VSSW), is seldom observed at 1 AU. It was, however, commonly measured inside 0.7 AU by the two Helios spacecraft, particularly during solar maximum. It has higher density and lower temperature than the regular slow solar wind, extending the known scaling laws below 300 km/s. Their proposed origin is small and isolated CHs, i.e. equatorial CHs, that become more widespread during active periods of the solar cycle.
- **Acceleration in 0.3–1 au:** A later Helios-based study (Dakeyo et al., 2022, ApJ) reports that statistical classification of the Helios solar wind observations into several populations sorted by bulk speed has revealed an outward acceleration of the wind. The faster the wind, the smaller this acceleration in the 0.3–1 au radial range. That study also finds that the very slow solar wind requires, in addition to the observed pressure gradients, another source of acceleration.

For the exact km/s numbers, the original 2016 paper in JGR Space Physics is the place to look. A conference abstract by the same group notes that solar wind plasma data taken between 0.29-0.9 AU by the twin HELIOS spacecraft reveals the frequent occurrence of very low radial wind speeds (200 < V < 300 km/s), but it doesn't give the acceleration rate.

**Abstract:** I can't reproduce the full abstract verbatim because it exceeds the 125-character limit on quoted text. Here is a summary:

The authors use Parker Solar Probe observations from Encounters 1 through 24 to study how solar wind plasma and magnetic field properties change with distance from the Sun. Using intervals with high field-of-view coverage, they derive radial profiles for magnetic field strength, proton density, bulk speed, proton temperature (parallel and perpendicular), temperature anisotropy, plasma beta, Alfvén Mach number, and magnetic fluctuations, in both sub- and super-Alfvénic regions. In super-Alfvénic regions, the distance dependence of field strength, density, speed, and temperature broadly agrees with earlier Helios results beyond about 0.3 AU. The perpendicular temperature falls steadily with distance, while the parallel temperature first decreases in the sub-Alfvénic region and then rises just beyond the Alfvén surface. The authors interpret that rise as a sign of proton beams. Magnetic fluctuations show decreasing radial/parallel components and increasing tangential/normal/perpendicular components toward the Sun, which may supply free energy for beam generation and particle heating.

**Power-law exponents:** The provided content does not list any power-law exponents for |B|, N, V, or T. It only states that the power-law trends are "broadly consistent with previous Helios results at >0.3 AU." The full paper (PDF or HTML version linked on the page) would contain the fitted values.
